content: 1. Estradiol/Norethindrone Acetate should not be used during lactation, as estrogen administration to nursing women has been shown to decrease both the quantity and quality of breast milk. Detectable amounts of estrogens and progestins have been identified in the breast milk of women receiving these drugs. Caution is advised when administering estradiol/norethindrone acetate to a nursing woman. 2. Estradiol/Norethindrone Acetate is not indicated for use in children, as clinical studies have not been conducted in the pediatric population. 3. There have not been sufficient numbers of geriatric women (over 65 years of age) included in studies of estradiol/norethindrone acetate to determine whether their response differs from that of younger subjects. In the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) studies, women over 65 years of age receiving estrogen plus progestin therapy had a higher relative risk of nonfatal stroke and invasive breast cancer. In the estrogen-alone sub-study, there was a higher relative risk of stroke in women over 65 years of age. Ancillary studies in postmenopausal women aged 65 to 79 years showed an increased risk of probable dementia in those receiving estrogen plus progestin or estrogen alone compared to placebo. It is unknown whether these findings apply to younger postmenopausal women. 4. There is no FDA guidance on the use of estradiol and norethindrone acetate (transdermal patch) with respect to specific gender populations, racial populations, patients with renal impairment, patients with hepatic impairment, women of reproductive potential, males, or immunocompromised patients. 5. The transdermal patch should be applied to a smooth, clean, dry area of the skin on the lower abdomen. It should not be applied to or near the breasts. The selected area should not be oily, damaged, or irritated, and the waistline should be avoided to prevent dislodgement or interference with drug delivery. Application sites must be rotated, with at least one week between applications to the same site. 6. To apply the patch, open the pouch, remove one side of the protective liner without touching the adhesive, and immediately apply the patch to the lower abdomen. Remove the second side of the liner and press the patch firmly in place for at least 10 seconds, ensuring good contact, especially around the edges. Care should be taken to prevent dislodgement during bathing or other activities. If the patch falls off, it may be reapplied to another area of the lower abdomen or replaced with a new patch, maintaining the original treatment schedule. Only one patch should be worn at a time during the 3to 4-day dosing interval. The patch should not be exposed to prolonged sunlight. 7. To remove the patch, do so carefully and slowly to avoid skin irritation. If adhesive residue remains, allow the area to dry for 15 minutes, then gently rub the area with an oil-based cream or lotion to remove the residue. 8. Overdosage of estrogen or estrogen plus progestin may cause nausea, vomiting, breast tenderness, abdominal pain, drowsiness, fatigue, and withdrawal bleeding in women. Treatment involves discontinuation of estradiol/norethindrone acetate therapy and appropriate symptomatic care. 9. Endogenous estrogens are primarily responsible for the development and maintenance of the female reproductive system and secondary sexual characteristics. Estradiol is the principal intracellular human estrogen and is significantly more potent than its metabolites, estrone and estriol, at the receptor level. In premenopausal women, the ovarian follicle is the primary source of estrogen, secreting 70 to 500 mcg of estradiol daily, depending on the menstrual cycle phase. After menopause, most endogenous estrogen is produced by the conversion of androstenedione, secreted by the adrenal cortex, to estrone in peripheral tissues. Estrone and its sulfate conjugate, estrone sulfate, are the most abundant circulating estrogens in postmenopausal women. 10. Estrogens act by binding to nuclear receptors in estrogen-responsive tissues. Two estrogen receptors have been identified, and their proportions vary across tissues. Circulating estrogens modulate the pituitary secretion of gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH), and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) through a negative feedback mechanism, reducing the elevated levels of these hormones seen in postmenopausal women. 11. Estradiol USP is a white to creamy white, odorless, crystalline powder with a molecular weight of 272.39 and a molecular formula of C18H24O2. Norethindrone Acetate (NETA) USP is a white to creamy white, odorless, crystalline powder with a molecular weight of 340.47 and a molecular formula of C22H28O3. 12. Estradiol used in hormone therapy is well absorbed through the skin, mucous membranes, and gastrointestinal tract. Administration of estradiol/norethindrone acetate every 3 to 4 days in postmenopausal women produces average steady-state estradiol serum concentrations of 45 to 50 pg/mL, which are within the normal range observed at the early follicular phase of the menstrual cycle.
